slides.label: Title
slides.notes: Open by making the contract explicit: this lecture is about implementation interfaces, not a new algebraic product. The chapter asks what happens after basis blades are already computable. We freeze an ordered basis, store multivectors as coordinates, and then decide when a matrix representation is helpful and when sparse distribution is the better engineering path.

slides.label: Lecture Map
slides.notes: Use this route slide to prevent students from treating the matrix construction as the whole chapter. The matrix view is a translation layer that exposes linearity and structure coefficients. The sparse list view is the implementation habit that keeps geometric algebra practical when most multivectors have only a few active basis blades.

slides.label: Coordinate Contract
slides.notes: Pause on the phrase coordinate contract. A vector of eight numbers is not a multivector until the order of basis blades is fixed and shared by every operation. The grade-first order is also a debugging aid: projections, triangular outer products, and contraction grade changes can be inspected directly by row and column blocks.

slides.label: Addition And Scaling
slides.notes: Keep this slide deliberately simple. Addition and scalar multiplication are the sanity checks for the representation layer. They only work entrywise because both columns use the same L list. When students later see product matrices, remind them that the matrix is more complicated, but the coordinate contract underneath has not changed.

slides.label: Grade Projection
slides.notes: Use the diagonal picture to connect grade extraction with ordinary linear algebra. Nothing about the coefficients is interpreted during projection; the operation only asks which basis blade lives in which grade. That is why the notebook can test reconstruction by adding all projected pieces and comparing back to the original coordinate column.

slides.label: Sign Operations
slides.notes: The important implementation point is that these operations are not arbitrary 8 by 8 matrices in the chosen basis. They are diagonal, grade-driven, and constant for the algebra. Students should see the table as generated data: once the grade of each basis blade is known, the signs can be produced mechanically and checked as involutions.

slides.label: Product Matrix
slides.notes: Stress the type distinction: A is a multivector, while the displayed matrix is the linear map obtained by fixing A as the left multiplier. This distinction prevents a common implementation mistake where the product itself is imagined as a single universal matrix. The matrix changes with A, but its sparsity pattern and routing rule come from basis-blade products.

slides.label: Structure Coefficients
slides.notes: Describe the routing as a sparse tensor lookup rather than as a mysterious formula. The pair of basis blades tells us which output basis blade appears and with what signed metric coefficient. Matrix assembly then places that scaled A coordinate in the cell where the corresponding B coordinate will multiply it during ordinary matrix-vector multiplication.

slides.label: Product Filters
slides.notes: Frame these as tables that differ by grade policy. The geometric product table routes every allowed basis product, while outer and contraction tables suppress rows that do not land in their target grade. This is why the matrices look related but not interchangeable, and why a test suite should compare each product kind separately.

slides.label: Contraction Variants
slides.notes: Contractions are where grade bookkeeping pays off. For a vector against a bivector, the left contraction keeps grade one and the outer product keeps grade three, so the geometric product visibly splits. Then contrast this with right contraction: it is not a synonym but the grade question asked from the other side of the product.

slides.label: Non-Diagonal Metric
slides.notes: This slide is a useful warning against overfitting to Euclidean diagonal examples. The clean sign-and-mask rule from basis blades remains valuable, but a non-diagonal metric can send one basis product into a small sum. The implementation should therefore store product results as sparse terms even when most classroom examples collapse to one blade.

slides.label: Sparse List
slides.notes: Connect the sparse loop to distributivity, then immediately connect it to cost. The dense matrix method is excellent for deriving and bootstrapping symbolic recipes, but a typical geometric object or versor has limited support. Sparse loops spend work on active basis-blade pairs, then simplify duplicates, which is the path toward the optimizations later chapters specialize.

slides.label: Implementation Tests
slides.notes: Present the checks as reusable engineering assets. They are not just confirmation that one notebook ran once; they encode invariants future implementations can steal. In particular, comparing matrix and sparse products is powerful because the two paths fail for different reasons. The non-diagonal metric check is especially useful for catching hidden orthogonality assumptions.

slides.label: Structural Prompts
slides.notes: Use these as active prompts rather than answers to recite. The goal is for students to read a product matrix geometrically: first by basis order, then by grade blocks, then by the surviving cells induced by a product rule. The right contraction prompt is a useful final check because it forces them to reverse the grade comparison deliberately.

slides.label: Recap
slides.notes: Close by tying the matrix view and sparse view together rather than ranking one as universally better. The matrix view is the conceptual and symbolic scaffold; the sparse view is the practical default for typical multivectors. Later specialization should be presented as preserving these contracts while compiling away unnecessary loops and zero work.
